# Reflections

I learnt how time-series data can be visualised using different techniques such as calendar heatmaps, cycle plots and slopegraphs. The calendar heatmap was especially useful because it combines the day and hour into one visual, making it easier to identify periods with higher activity. I also learnt how functions such as `lubridate`, `group_by()` and `facet_wrap()` can be used to prepare time-related data and compare patterns across different groups.

# Introduction

By the end of this hands-on exercise, we will be able to use R packages to create several types of time-oriented data visualisations, including:

-   Calendar heatmaps using `ggplot2`

-   Cycle plots using `ggplot2`

-   Slopegraphs

-   Horizon charts

# Getting started

## Installing and loading R packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(scales, viridis, lubridate, ggthemes,
               gridExtra, readxl, knitr, data.table,
               CGPfunctions, ggHoriPlot, tidyverse)
```
:::


# Plotting calendar heatmap

In this section, we will learn how to plot a calender heatmap by using ggplot2 package.

## The Data

eventlog.csv file will be used. This data file consists of 199,999 rows of time-series cyber attack records by country.

## Importing the data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")
```
:::


## Examine the data structure

kable() can be used to review the structure of the imported data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|timestamp           |source_country |tz              |
|:-------------------|:--------------|:---------------|
|2015-03-12 15:59:16 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:00:48 |FR             |Europe/Paris    |
|2015-03-12 16:02:26 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:02:38 |US             |America/Chicago |
|2015-03-12 16:03:22 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |
|2015-03-12 16:03:45 |CN             |Asia/Shanghai   |


:::
:::


The dataset contains three columns: `timestamp`, `source_country`, and `tz`.

-   `timestamp` records the date and time of each attack in POSIXct format.

-   `source_country` indicates the country where the attack originated, represented using the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code.

-   `tz` represents the time zone associated with the source IP address.

## Data preparation

### 1. Deriving weekday and hour of day fields

Two new fields namely *wkday* and *hour* need to be derived. In this step, we will write a function to perform the task.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, 
                        tz = tz[1], 
                        quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(source_country = sc,
                   wkday = weekdays(real_times),
                   hour = hour(real_times))
  return(dt)
}
```
:::


**Note:** The `ymd_hms()` and `hour()` functions are provided by the **lubridate** package, which is loaded using `pacman::p_load()`. The `weekdays()` function is available in base R, so no additional package is required.

### 2. Deriving the attacks tibble data frame


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
wkday_levels <- c('Saturday', 'Friday', 
                  'Thursday', 'Wednesday', 
                  'Tuesday', 'Monday', 
                  'Sunday')

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, 
                   .$source_country, 
                   .$tz)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(wkday = factor(
    wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(
      hour, levels = 0:23))
```
:::


Beside extracting the necessary data into *attacks* data frame, `mutate()` of **dplyr** package is used to convert *wkday* and *hour* fields into **factor** so they’ll be ordered when plotting

Table below shows the tidy tibble table after processing.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
kable(head(attacks))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|tz           |source_country |wkday    |hour |
|:------------|:--------------|:--------|:----|
|Africa/Cairo |BG             |Saturday |20   |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |6    |
|Africa/Cairo |TW             |Sunday   |8    |
|Africa/Cairo |CN             |Sunday   |11   |
|Africa/Cairo |US             |Sunday   |15   |
|Africa/Cairo |CA             |Monday   |11   |


:::
:::


## Building Calendar heatmaps


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
grouped <- attacks %>% 
  count(wkday, hour) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  na.omit()

ggplot(grouped, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
coord_equal() +
scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
labs(x = NULL, 
     y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
      legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The code first groups the attack records by weekday and hour, then counts the number of attacks for each combination. Missing values are removed before `geom_tile()` is used to create the heatmap. `theme_tufte()` simplifies the chart design, `coord_equal()` keeps the tiles evenly proportioned, and `scale_fill_gradient()` uses colour intensity to represent the number of attacks.

Then we can simply group the count by hour and wkday and plot it, since we know that we have values for every combination there’s no need to further preprocess the data.

## Building multiple calendar heatmaps

We will be building multiple heatmaps for the top four countries with the highest number of attacks.

### Plotting multiple calendar heatmaps

#### 1. Deriving attack by country object

To identify top 4 countries with highest number of attacks we need to:

-   count the number of attacks by country,

-   calculate the percent of attackes by country, and

-   save the results in a tibble data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
attacks_by_country <- count(
  attacks, source_country) %>%
  mutate(percent = percent(n/sum(n))) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))
```
:::


#### 2. Preparing the tidy data frame

We are required to extract the attack records of the top 4 countries from *attacks* data frame and save the data in a new tibble data frame (i.e. *top4_attacks*).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
top4 <- attacks_by_country$source_country[1:4]
top4_attacks <- attacks %>%
  filter(source_country %in% top4) %>%
  count(source_country, wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(source_country = factor(
    source_country, levels = top4)) %>%
  na.omit()
```
:::


#### 3. Plotting multiple calendar heatmap by using ggplot2 package


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(top4_attacks, 
       aes(hour, 
           wkday, 
           fill = n)) + 
  geom_tile(color = "white", 
          size = 0.1) + 
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") + 
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks",
                    low = "sky blue", 
                    high = "dark blue") +
  facet_wrap(~source_country, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, 
     title = "Attacks on top 4 countries by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 6) )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


# Plotting cycle plot

We will learn how to plot a cycle plot showing the time-series patterns and trend of visitor arrivals from Vietnam programmatically by using ggplot2 functions.

## 1. Data import

arrivals_by_air.xlsx will be used.

The code chunk below imports arrivals_by_air.xlsx by using read_excel() of readxl package and save it as a tibble data frame called air.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air <- read_excel("data/arrivals_by_air.xlsx")
```
:::


## 2. Deriving month and year fields

Next, two new fields called month and year are derived from Month-Year field.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
air$month <- factor(month(air$`Month-Year`), 
                    levels=1:12, 
                    labels=month.abb, 
                    ordered=TRUE) 
air$year <- year(ymd(air$`Month-Year`))
```
:::


## 3. Extracting target country

Next, the code chunk below is use to extract data for the target country (i.e. Vietnam)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
Vietnam <- air %>% 
  select(`Vietnam`, 
         month, 
         year) %>%
  filter(year >= 2010)
```
:::


## 4. Computing year average arrivals by month

The code chunk below uses group_by() and summarise() of dplyr to compute year average arrivals by month.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hline.data <- Vietnam %>% 
  group_by(month) %>%
  summarise(avgvalue = mean(`Vietnam`))
```
:::


## 5. Plotting the cycle plot

The code chunk below is used to plot the cycle plot


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data=Vietnam,
            aes(x=year, 
                y=`Vietnam`, 
                group=month), 
            colour="black") +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept=avgvalue), 
             data=hline.data, 
             linetype=6, 
             colour="red", 
             size=0.5) + 
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
       title = "Visitor arrivals from Vietnam by air, Jan 2010-Dec 2019") +
  xlab("") +
  ylab("No. of Visitors") +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


# Plotting slopegraph

In this section wewill learn how to plot a [slopegraph](https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/blog/2020/7/27/what-is-a-slopegraph) by using R.

Before getting start, make sure that **CGPfunctions** has been installed and loaded onto R environment. Then, refer to [Using newggslopegraph](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CGPfunctions/vignettes/Using-newggslopegraph.html) to learn more about the function. Lastly, read more about `newggslopegraph()` and its arguments by referring to this [link](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/CGPfunctions/versions/0.6.3/topics/newggslopegraph).
